newsitem.title: FRANCE: Protesters mass for French far-right congress.
newsitem.headline: Protesters mass for French far-right congress.

text.p: Members of France's far-right National Front, hoping for an election breakthrough next year, gathered for their congress on Saturday amid heavy security as thousands of foes massed nearby for a protest march.

Row upon row of riot police sealed off the conference centre in the eastern city of Strasbourg, reluctant host to the three-day meeting of Jean-Marie Le Pen's anti-immigrant party which also deployed its own burly security guards.

Socialist mayor Catherine Trautmann has called in 2,000 police and appealed for calm even as she vowed to lead the afternoon protest, which organisers said would draw more than 50,000 people from across the country, Germany and Switzerland.
The march was due to start at 3 p.m. (1400 GMT), half an hour after the congress opening.
As protesters poured in from chartered trains, Front leaders advised the 2,200 delegates to remain closeted in the congress and warned authorities they would be responsible for any violence.
"They are trying to frighten us, but we won't respond," said 20-year old Front delegate Laetitia Firek.
A protest banner bearing a Nazi swastika was briefly hoisted on the spire of the towering Gothic cathedral as local officials visited the site of a synagogue burnt down by the Nazis in World War Two.
Representatives of the MRAP anti-racist group laid a wreath at the site of the Struthof Nazi World War Two concentration camp, near Strasbourg, where some 25,000 died.

City authorities put up giant posters outside the conference centre proclaiming in a myriad of languages the motto of the French Republic "liberty, equality, fraternity". Anti-Front protesters also planted black flowers and painted black bands on street signs, saying they were "mourning democracy".

The Strasbourg march caps a groundswell of opposition to Le Pen which was fuelled by the Front winning control of a fourth French town, Vitrolles, in a municipal by-election last month, and by protests at a government hardline anti-immigration law.
The feisty Le Pen, who won 15 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential poll, has vowed an assault on the political establishment in the run-up to a March 1998 general election.

France's first-past-the-post election system has barred the Front from parliament, but Le Pen he says he is confident it can ride to power on the back of record 12.8 percent unemployment and simmering resentment of North African immigrants and political corruption.
The Front calls for sending immigrants home and giving preference to French nationals for jobs and social benefits.
A survey in the weekly Le Point said that the Front would poll 15 percent of the votes, up from 12.5 percent in 1993, but would remain out of parliament if the election were held now.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin and Communist chief Robert Hue, who were to take part in the protest march, denounced the Front in interviews published by the daily Le Parisien on Saturday, as racist, xenophobic, anti-Semitic and fascist.

"Contrary to what one government representative said in appealing for 'respect of all opinions', we mustn't respect the ideas of the extreme-right, we have to fight them. Racism and anti-Semitism are not 'opinions' but offences," Jospin said.

Politicians disagree on how to counter the Front's rise, with the ruling centre-right coalition refusing to participate in the march and President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist Rally for the Republic arguing that protests play into Le Pen's hands.
Many analysts agreed that the protests would mainly serve to keep the Front and its controversial agenda in the public eye.

"In choosing to hold his congress in Strasbourg, Jean-Marie Le Pen has certainly achieved his top goal: to win the largest possible media and public exposure," said the regional daily Dernieres Nouvelles d'Alsace in a front-page editorial.
The congress was convened to re-elect Le Pen as president, choose a central committee, write an election platform and set out a campaign strategy.
Le Pen, the party's 68-year-old founder, is unopposed for president and has refused to discuss a successor.
The previous National Front congress, held in suburban Paris five years ago, adopted a platform of "300 measures for the rebirth of France".
